big_idea: Most organizational strategy is actually fluff, goal-setting, or a list of aspirations dressed up as strategy; real strategy is a coherent response built on an honest diagnosis of the specific obstacle standing in the way.

tool.label: The Kernel of Good Strategy
tool.text: Rumelt argues every good strategy has the same three-part structure. First, a diagnosis that simplifies a complex situation down to the one or two critical factors actually determining outcomes -- Rumelt claims 80% of strategy work is in the diagnosis. Second, a guiding policy -- a general approach for dealing with the obstacle, like highway guardrails that channel action. Third, coherent actions -- coordinated, mutually reinforcing steps that carry out the guiding policy, rather than a wish list of disconnected initiatives.
tool.note: The book is much stronger at diagnosing bad strategy than at teaching readers to construct good strategy from scratch -- it reads more like a rigorous critique toolkit than a step-by-step generative method.

ideas.title: The four hallmarks of bad strategy
ideas.text: Fluff, failure to face the challenge, mistaking goals for strategy, and bad strategic objectives that are either too vague or an unprioritized laundry list.

ideas.title: Strategy as leverage
ideas.text: Good strategy concentrates limited resources and attention at a pivot point where a small, well-aimed push produces disproportionate results.

ideas.title: The importance of a proximate objective
ideas.text: When a problem is too complex or uncertain, strong strategy narrows focus to an achievable near-term objective.

ideas.title: Chain-link systems
ideas.text: Some organizations' performance is governed by their weakest link, not their average performance.

ideas.title: Using your advantage / exploiting inertia
ideas.text: Good strategy often works by identifying where competitors are structurally slow or unable to respond.

ideas.title: Strategic vs. administrative thinking
ideas.text: Rumelt distinguishes strategy (choosing where and how to compete) from mere planning and budgeting.

try_it: Write a one-paragraph diagnosis of the single biggest obstacle facing your team or business right now, without listing any solutions yet.
Audit your last strategy document for fluff -- buzzwords or restated goals with no actual causal logic -- and cut anything that doesn't survive.
Pick one current initiative and check whether its stated actions are actually coordinated with each other, or just a bundled wish list.
Identify the weakest link constraining your team's output and redirect one resource allocation toward it instead of your strongest area.
best_for: Senior operators and executives who already write strategy documents but suspect their own strategy is really just a budget and aspirational goals.
Consultants and strategy leads who need a sharp, repeatable diagnostic lens for critiquing weak plans.
less_useful: First-time managers with no existing strategy process to critique, who need step-by-step how-to guidance more.
Readers hoping for a workbook-style, fill-in-the-template approach.

related.why: Blue Ocean Strategy offers a more generative counterpart to this book's diagnostic rigor.
Playing to Win shares Rumelt's insistence that strategy means hard, exclusionary choices.
